name: Numbers, Time & Money
description: Build fluent, automatic handling of numbers, prices, times, dates and quantities.

runtime_inputs.name: Area to focus on
runtime_inputs.prompt: Is there a part of this you want to focus on — numbers, prices, times, dates — or shall I pick?

objectives.description: Understand spoken numbers on first hearing.
success_indicators: writes down or repeats a number correctly without a second hearing

objectives.description: Produce numbers aloud without counting up to them.
success_indicators: says a two-digit number without hesitation
says a three or four digit number correctly

objectives.description: Understand a price when it is said aloud.
success_indicators: repeats a price back correctly, including the small units

objectives.description: State a price, including decimals or small units.
success_indicators: produces a price in the natural form used by native speakers

objectives.description: Understand a time when it is said aloud.
success_indicators: acts correctly on a stated time
uses the idiomatic form rather than digit-by-digit
gives a date in the usual order for the language

objectives.description: Use numbers with quantities and counters.
success_indicators: combines a number with the right counter or unit

objectives.description: Get through a short real transaction involving money.
success_indicators: understands a total and responds appropriately

teaching_philosophy: Numbers are a fluency problem, not a knowledge problem. Aim for automatic.
Retrieval over explanation. Short prompts, fast turns, many repetitions.
Reliability before range: never extend while smaller numbers are still slow.
Keep your turns very short here. They should be doing most of the talking.
Practise numbers in frames people really use - a price, a time, an age, a phone number, a platform. Never pad a number into an invented sentence just to make a sentence.
A bare number said quickly and correctly is worth more than a nonsense sentence containing it.

target_vocabulary: the currency and its small unit
how much, how many, what time
suggested_vocabulary: first, second, third and the ordinal pattern
a half, a third, a quarter
in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening
a dozen, a pair, a couple of
target_grammar: the idiomatic way of telling the time in this language
date order and any required prepositions
counters, classifiers or plural agreement where the language requires them
question forms for how much and how many

scenarios.name: Buying something small
scenarios.description: A short purchase: price, payment, change.

scenarios.name: Making an appointment
scenarios.description: Agreeing a day and a time.

scenarios.name: Exchanging a phone number
scenarios.description: Digits said quickly, then read back.

scenarios.name: Splitting a bill
scenarios.description: Arithmetic out loud, in the target language.

phases.name: Numbers
phases.purpose: Numbers up to 99, said without stopping to think.
instructions: Items are numbers. The meaning of each is the figure, for example 47.
If the student already knows the numbers up to a hundred, skip single digits: use two-digit numbers, and the readings people get wrong (4, 7 and 9).
The role-play is a situation where numbers are said aloud: a queue ticket, a room number, an age.

activities.name: Say it back
activities.description: You say a number at natural speed; the student repeats it.

activities.name: Count on
activities.description: You give a number; the student gives the next two.

entry_guidance: Start below where you think they are. Speed matters more than range.
advancement_guidance: Two-digit numbers come back without a pause.

phases.name: Larger numbers
phases.purpose: Hundreds and thousands, including the hundreds whose sound changes.
instructions: Items are numbers of the size prices come in: 300, 650, 1200, 8000.
Include at least one of 300, 600 or 800.

activities.name: Building a big number
activities.description: Assemble a number from its parts, out loud.

entry_guidance: Skip entirely for an absolute beginner.
advancement_guidance: Three-digit numbers are produced without assembly.

phases.name: Prices
phases.purpose: Asking what something costs and understanding the answer.
instructions: The first item is how to ask what something costs ("kore wa ikura desu ka"). Its reply is a price in words ("sen nihyaku en desu", reply_meaning "1200 yen"): the student is asked what price they heard. Then two or three prices to understand and say, and "I'll take this".

The role-play is a shop: the assistant states a price, and the student answers with "I'll take this". Asking the price is the customer's line, never the assistant's. The assistant's prices are different figures from the items.

activities.name: Price echo
activities.description: Repeat a price, then change it.

advancement_guidance: Prices with small units come back correctly.

phases.name: Time
phases.purpose: Asking the time and telling it: the hour, half past, and minutes.
instructions: Build a time up one piece at a time, each item one step on from the last: asking the time ("ima nanji desu ka", whose reply is a plain hour such as "sanji desu", reply_meaning "3:00"); then a plain hour ("sanji" — 3 o'clock; its note says an hour is the number and then ji); then half past the same hour ("sanji han" — 3:30; note: han is half); then one time with minutes ("kuji juppun" — 9:10; note: the minutes come after the hour).
No am or pm in this part — that is the next part — and no item longer than three words. At most one irregular hour (yoji, shichiji or kuji).

activities.name: Their actual day
activities.description: What time they get up, eat, finish work.

advancement_guidance: Times are produced idiomatically without translating from digits.

phases.name: Opening hours
phases.purpose: From what time until what time: shops, trains and restaurants.
instructions: Cover from and until, morning and afternoon, and asking what time something opens or leaves.
advancement_guidance: A date is produced in the right order without prompting.

phases.name: Paying
phases.purpose: Paying for something: card or cash, change, a receipt, no bag.
instructions: What a visitor says at the till: by card, in cash, can I use a card, a receipt please, no bag needed. Not "keep the change": there is no tipping in Japan.
The role-play is the till: the cashier asks, the student answers.

activities.name: Buying something
activities.description: Ask the price, hear the total, pay, take change.

phases.name: A whole purchase
phases.purpose: One visit to a shop from asking the price to paying, using everything so far.
instructions: Play the shop assistant. Use prices and phrases the student has been taught.

activities.name: Rapid switching
activities.description: A price, then a time, then a quantity, in quick succession.

entry_guidance: Only when the individual types are solid.

phases.name: Review
phases.purpose: Everything from this lesson, from memory.
instructions: Ask for each thing from its English.
Then say what they can now do.

activities.name: Conversation with numbers in it
activities.description: Ordinary talk that happens to be full of figures.

completion_guidance: Name the one number type still worth practising.

if_struggling: Narrow the range rather than slowing the pace; ten fast numbers beat thirty slow ones.
Drop back to the previous phase without commenting on it.
Use round figures until they are automatic.
Give the student the number in writing-order first, then ask for it aloud.
Spend a whole phase on one number type instead of moving through the progression.
if_succeeding: Speed up. This lesson's difficulty knob is pace.
Extend the range: bigger numbers, awkward prices, minutes that are not multiples of five.
Move to mixed practice early and stay there.

basis: how far through the progression the lesson has moved
whether numbers are produced without visible assembly
progress.notes: Approximate. Never state a percentage to the student.

criteria: numbers are understood on first hearing and produced without counting up
a time and a price have both been handled correctly
one real transaction has been completed unaided
announcement_guidance: Say concretely what got faster, since speed is the point of this lesson.

observe: which number ranges are still slow
whether times are produced idiomatically or digit by digit
any specific number form that failed repeatedly
counters or units the student omits
memory.notes: Ordinary weakness observations. Record them as weaknesses, not as a numbers-specific store.
